en: Thus have I heard— The Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, Discourse 82 of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kurus together with a large community of monks, he arrived at a market town of the Kurus named Thullakoṭṭhika.
The brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika heard:

"It is said, sirs, that the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, while wandering on tour among the Kurus together with a large community of monks, has arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika."
Furthermore, this excellent report concerning Master Gotama has spread abroad:

"Such indeed is that Blessed One—worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life (brahmacariya) in its entirety, complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Some, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side;
some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and having concluded the polite and courteous conversation, sat down to one side;
some extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side; and some [sat down] in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having announced their names and clans, some sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence.
As the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhita were sitting there to one side, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Now at that time, a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of a prominent family in that very Thullakoṭṭhita, was sitting in that assembly.
Then this thought occurred to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla:
“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to practice the holy life in its complete fullness, in its complete purity, polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?”
Then the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma,
rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words; rising from their seats, they paid homage to the Blessed One,
circumambulated him keeping him to their right, and departed.
Then, not long after the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika had departed, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living in a household to lead the holy life in its complete fullness, in its utter purity, polished like a conch shell.
Venerable sir, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, venerable sir; may I receive the full admission.”
“May the Blessed One let me go forth.
“But have you been permitted by your parents, Raṭṭhapāla, to go forth from the home life into homelessness?
“Venerable sir, I have not been permitted by my parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
“Ratthapāla, the Tathāgatas do not ordain a son without the permission of his parents.
“Venerable sir, I shall act in such a way that my parents will give me their permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Then the young man Ratthapāla rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, he approached his parents. Having approached them, he said this to his parents:

“Mother and father, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) that is utterly complete, utterly pure, polished like a conch shell.
I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Please grant me permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
When this was said, the parents of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said this to him:
“Dear Raṭṭhapāla, you are our only son, dear and beloved, raised in comfort and nurtured in luxury.
You, dear Raṭṭhapāla, know nothing of suffering.”

“Even by death we shall be separated from you against our will; how much less shall we grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness while you are still living? A second time, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla … [as before] … said: “I am not going to give up my intention. A third time, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said to his parents: “Mother and father, listen! This is my final word: I am not going to give up my intention. Then his parents said to him: “Son, you have always been our only child, dear and beloved, pleasing and charming, who has never done anything to displease us. You have been brought up in comfort, clothed in fine clothes, fed on fine food, with a lute in your hand, never having to experience hunger or thirst. How can you now go forth from the home life into homelessness? Son, do not go forth from the home life into homelessness!

A third time, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said to his parents: “Mother and father, listen! This is my final word: I am not going to give up my intention. Then his parents said to him: “Son, you have always been our only child, dear and beloved, pleasing and charming, who has never done anything to displease us. You have been brought up in comfort, clothed in fine clothes, fed on fine food, with a lute in your hand, never having to experience hunger or thirst. How can you now go forth from the home life into homelessness? Son, do not go forth from the home life into homelessness! Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla, being unable to persuade his parents to grant him permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness, rose from his seat and went away. He went to the Blessed One and, having approached, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I have informed my parents that I wish to go forth from the home life into homelessness under the Blessed One. But they did not grant me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Come, Ānanda, go to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla and say this to him: ‘Friend Raṭṭhapāla, the Teacher calls you; the Teacher summons you. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied, and he went to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla and said to him: “Friend Raṭṭhapāla, the Teacher calls you; the Teacher summons you. “Very well, friend,” the clansman Raṭṭhapāla replied, and he went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to him: “Raṭṭhapāla, your parents have not given you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness. “Venerable sir, even if my parents had given me permission, I would still not have gone forth from the home life into homelessness under the Blessed One. However, I have heard this: ‘When the Tathāgata summons someone, it is for their benefit, not for their harm. Therefore, venerable sir, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness. “Raṭṭhapāla, your parents have not given you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness. “Venerable sir, even if my parents had given me permission, I would still not have gone forth from the home life into homelessness under the Blessed One. A third time, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said this to his mother and father:

“Mother and father, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to practice the holy life in its absolute fullness, absolute purity, and total perfection, like a polished shell.
I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
“Grant me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For a third time, the noble son Raṭṭhapāla’s mother and father said this to him:
“Dear Raṭṭhapāla, you are our only son, beloved and dear, raised in comfort and brought up in luxury.”
"My dear Raṭṭhapāla, you do not know anything of suffering.
Even at your death we would be parted against our will;
how much less shall we permit you, while you are still living, to go forth from the home life into homelessness?"
Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla,
thinking, “My parents do not give me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness,” lay down right there on the bare ground,
saying: “Right here shall be my death, or my going forth.”
Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla did not eat even one meal; he did not eat two meals;
he did not eat three meals; he did not eat four meals; he did not eat five meals; he did not eat six meals; he did not eat seven meals.
Then the mother and father of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said this to him:
“Dear Raṭṭhapāla, you are our only son, dear and beloved, raised in comfort and brought up in luxury.
You do not know anything of suffering, dear Raṭṭhapāla.”
"Even by death shall we be separated from you against our will.
How much less shall we permit you, while you are still living, to go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Arise, dear Raṭṭhapāla! Eat, drink, and enjoy yourself!"
"Enjoy yourself! Drink, attend to your pleasures, indulge in sensual desires, and perform meritorious deeds; take your delight.
We do not permit you to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Even by death we shall be parted against our will."
“But how could we possibly permit him to go forth from the home life into homelessness while he is still living?
When this was said, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla remained silent.

A second time, the mother and father of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla spoke thus to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla … [as before] … *Note: The ellipsis (*...*) indicates that the text repeats the preceding dialogue.*
A second time, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla remained silent.
A third time, the mother and father of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said this to him:
“Dear Raṭṭhapāla, you are our only son, beloved and dear to us, raised in comfort and brought up in luxury.”
"My dear Raṭṭhapāla, you know nothing of suffering.
Even at your death we would be parted against our will; how much less shall we permit you, while you are still living, to go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Arise, my dear Raṭṭhapāla! Eat, drink, and enjoy yourself!"
"Enjoy yourself, drinking, feasting, and indulging in sensual pleasures; perform meritorious deeds and take your delight.
We do not permit you to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Even by death we shall be parted from you against our will."
“But how could we possibly permit him, while he is still living, to go forth from the home life into homelessness?
For a third time, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla remained silent.
Then the companions of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the clansman Raṭṭhapāla; having approached, they said this to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla:
“Friend Raṭṭhapāla, you are your mother and father’s only son—dear, beloved, raised in comfort, and brought up in luxury.
You, friend Raṭṭhapāla, know nothing of suffering.
Even by death your mother and father will be separated from you against their will.”
But how will they allow you to go forth from the home life into homelessness while you are still living?
Get up, dear Raṭṭhapāla! Eat, drink, and enjoy yourself;
while eating, drinking, and enjoying yourself, delighting in sensual pleasures and performing meritorious deeds, may you find happiness.
“Your parents will not grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Even through death, your parents will eventually be parted from you against their will;
how much less will they grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness while you are still alive?”
When this was said, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla remained silent.
A second time… and a third time,
the companions of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said this to him:
“My dear Raṭṭhapāla, you are your mother and father’s only son—dear, beloved, raised in comfort, and brought up in luxury.
You, my dear Raṭṭhapāla, know nothing of suffering; even at your death, your mother and father would be unwilling to be parted from you.
How much less will they grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness while you are still living?”

“Arise, dear Raṭṭhapāla! Eat, drink, and enjoy yourself! While eating, drinking, and enjoying yourself, and while indulging in sensual pleasures and performing meritorious deeds, you shall find delight.
Your parents will not grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness; even at death, your parents would be unwilling to be parted from you.
How much less, then, would they grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness while you are still living?”
A third time, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla remained silent.
Then the companions of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the parents of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla; having approached, they said this to the parents of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla:
“Mother and father, this clansman Raṭṭhapāla is lying right there on the bare ground:”
“Either death will come to me right here, or the going forth.
If you do not grant the noble son Raṭṭhapāla permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness, death will come to him right there.
But if you grant the noble son Raṭṭhapāla permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness, you will see him even after he has gone forth.
“If the clansman Raṭṭhapāla does not find delight in going forth from the home life into homelessness, what other destination could he have? He will surely return right here.
Grant permission for the clansman Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“We grant permission, dear friend, for the clansman Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
“Furthermore, one who has gone forth must show his gratitude to his mother and father.
Then the companions of the young man Raṭṭhapāla approached him and, having approached, said this to the young man Raṭṭhapāla:
“Arise, friend Raṭṭhapāla! You have been permitted by your mother and father to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
“Furthermore, once you have gone forth, you must look after your mother and father.
Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla rose, summoned his strength, and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Raṭṭhapāla...
The son of good family said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have been permitted by my mother and father to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
May the Blessed One grant me the going forth.”
The clansman Raṭṭhapāla received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Thullakoṭṭhika for as long as he pleased with the venerable Raṭṭhapāla—who had been ordained not long ago, having received full ordination only half a month—set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute,
before long attained that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, he entered and dwelt therein. He declared:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla became one of the Arahants.

Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I wish to visit my mother and father, if the Blessed One grants me permission.
Then the Blessed One, with his own mind, encompassed the mind of the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla.
When the Blessed One knew,
“The clansman Raṭṭhapāla is incapable of abandoning the training and returning to the lower life,” he then said to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla,
“Raṭṭhapāla, you may go now at whatever time you deem appropriate.”

Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, he put his lodging in order, took his bowl and robe, and set out on a wandering tour toward Thullakoṭṭhika.
Wandering by stages, he eventually arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika.
There, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dwelt at Thullakoṭṭhika in King Koravya’s Migacīra Park.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms.
While walking for alms from house to house in Thullakoṭṭhika, he approached his own father’s residence.
Now at that time, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father was having the middle door-hall plastered.
The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father saw the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar.
Upon seeing him, he said this:
“Our only son, dear and beloved to us, has been made to go forth by these shaveling ascetics!”
Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla received neither an offering nor a refusal at his father’s residence;
instead, he received nothing but abuse.
At that time, a female slave belonging to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s relatives was wishing to throw away some porridge left over from the previous day.
Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to that female slave of his relatives:
"Sister, if this is food fit to be discarded, pour it here into my bowl.

Then, as the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s female slave of his relatives was pouring that overnight sour gruel into the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s bowl, she took note of the appearance of his hands, his feet, and his voice.
Then a female slave belonging to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s relatives approached the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s mother; having approached, she said this to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s mother:
“Please know, madam, that Master Raṭṭhapāla has arrived.”
“If you speak the truth, my son, I shall make you a slave.
Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s mother approached the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father; having approached, she said this to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father:
“Please, householder, you should know this:”
“Is it true that the clansman Raṭṭhapāla has arrived?
At that time, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was eating that overnight sour gruel by the base of a certain wall.
Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father approached the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
“Is it possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that you will eat last night’s sour gruel?
Surely, dear Raṭṭhapāla, you ought to go to your own home?
“Householder, where would we have a home for us who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness?”
“We are homeless ones, householder.
We went to your house, householder, but there we received neither alms nor an invitation;
instead, we received nothing but abuse.”
“Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let us go home.
“Enough, householder; my meal-duty for today is finished.
“In that case, dear Raṭṭhapāla, please accept a meal from us tomorrow.”
The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla consented by remaining silent.
Then, having understood the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s consent, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father went to his own residence;
having arrived, he had a great heap of gold and bullion prepared.
Having covered [the house] with mats of kilañja grass, the former wife of the venerable Raṭṭhapāla addressed her daughters-in-law:
“Come, daughters-in-law, adorn yourselves with that same ornament with which you were formerly dear and pleasing to the noble son Raṭṭhapāla.
Then, at the end of that night, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father had exquisite hard and soft food prepared in his own residence and announced the time to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla.
“It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla; the meal is ready.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to his father’s residence.
Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then, as the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla—
The father had a heap of gold and bullion uncovered and said this to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
“This, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is your mother’s wealth of clay; one part is from your father, and another from your grandfather.
It is possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, both to enjoy wealth and to perform meritorious deeds.”
“Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, return to the low life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
“If you were to do as I say, householder, you would have this heap of gold and bullion loaded onto carts, transported out, and dumped into the middle of the Ganges River’s current. Why is that?”
“For those sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs, householder, will arise for you on that account.
Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s former wife, having grasped his feet one by one, said this to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
“What kind of nymphs, noble son, are they for whose sake you lead the holy life?”
“Sister, we do not lead the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs.
“The noble son Raṭṭhapāla addresses us as ‘sisters,’” they said, and right there they fainted and fell down.
Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to his father:
“If food is to be given, householder, give it;
do not trouble us.
“Eat, dear Raṭṭhapāla; the meal is ready,” he said.
Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father, with his own hands, satisfied and served the venerable Raṭṭhapāla with various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft.
When the venerable Raṭṭhapāla had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, he stood right there and recited these verses:
“Behold this crafted image, ... [the rest of the verse] ...”
This body is a heap of sores,
afflicted, full of many anxieties,
and there is no permanence in its stability.
Behold this body adorned with jewels and earrings,
yet covered only by skin over its bones.
She shines with her garments;
her feet are dyed with red lac,
and her face is smeared with cosmetic powder.
Enough for the delusion of the fool,
but not for one who seeks the further shore;
his hair is trimmed into the eightfold pattern.
The eyes are smeared with collyrium;
it is sufficient for the delusion of the fool,
but not for one who seeks the further shore.
Like a fresh collyrium box,
this putrid body is adorned;
it is sufficient to delude the fool.
Yet they do not seek the further shore.
The hunter set his snare,
but the deer did not spring the trap.
“Having eaten our fodder, we go, while the deer-trappers wail.

Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having spoken these verses while standing right there, approached King Koravya’s Deer Park; having arrived, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then King Koravya addressed Migava:
“Clear the deer-park grounds of the pleasure grove, dear Migava;
let us go to see the beautiful terrain.”
“Yes, Your Majesty,” Migava replied to King Koravya. While clearing the Deer Park, he saw the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla sitting at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Having seen him, he approached King Koravya and said to him:
“Your Majesty, the Deer Park has been cleared.”

“There is a clansman here named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of a prominent family in this very Thullakoṭṭhika, whom you have been constantly praising; he is sitting at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
“In that case, friend Migava, enough of going to the park today.
Let us now go and attend upon that venerable Raṭṭhapāla.”
Then King Koravya, having said, "Let all the solid and soft food prepared there be distributed," had fine carriages harnessed; mounting a fine carriage,
he set out from Thullakoṭṭhika with a great royal retinue in fine carriages to see the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla.
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground was passable for a carriage, he alighted from the carriage and approached the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla on foot, accompanied by his retinue in full array.
Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side. Standing to one side...
King Koravya, standing there, said this to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
“May the venerable Raṭṭhapāla sit here on the elephant rug.
“Enough, great king; you sit down yourself.”
“I am seated on my own seat.
King Koravya sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, King Koravya said this to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
“Master Raṭṭhapāla, there are these four kinds of loss, possessed of which some people here shave off their hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
Which four?
Loss through aging, loss through illness, loss of wealth, and loss of relatives.
And what, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is loss through aging?
In this case, Master Raṭṭhapāla, a certain person is aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life.
He reflects thus:
‘I am now aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life.’
‘It is not easy for me to acquire wealth not yet acquired, nor to increase wealth already acquired.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?
Being thus afflicted by the loss of his youth, he shaves off his hair and beard, dons saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
This, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is called the loss through old age.
But you, Master Raṭṭhapāla, are now young, a youth with beautiful black hair, endowed with the prime of youth and in the first stage of life.
That loss through old age does not yet exist for you, Master Raṭṭhapāla.
"What has Master Raṭṭhapāla known, seen, or heard that he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness?
And what, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is the loss through illness?
Here, Master Raṭṭhapāla, a certain person is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill."
Thus he reflects:
"At present I am afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
It is not easy for me to acquire wealth not yet acquired, nor to increase wealth already acquired."
"What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don yellow robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Being thus afflicted by that loss through illness, he shaves off his hair and beard, dons yellow robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
This, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is called "loss through illness."
Moreover, Master Raṭṭhapāla is currently free from illness and affliction, possessing a digestive system that is well-balanced, being neither too cold nor too hot.
Thus, Master Raṭṭhapāla has no loss due to disease.
What did Master Raṭṭhapāla know, or see, or hear, that he went forth from the home life into homelessness?
And what, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is the loss of wealth?
Here, Master Raṭṭhapāla, a certain person is wealthy, possessing great riches and great wealth.
Those riches of his gradually go to complete exhaustion.
Thus he reflects:
"In the past, I was wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments.
Those possessions of mine have gradually come to exhaustion."
‘It is not easy for me, with wealth unattained to acquire it, or with wealth already acquired to increase it.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Thus, being possessed of that loss of wealth, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
This, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is called the loss of wealth.
But as for you, Master Raṭṭhapāla, you are the son of a preeminent family right here in Thullakoṭṭhika;
that loss of wealth does not apply to you, Master Raṭṭhapāla.
"What has Master Raṭṭhapāla known, seen, or heard that he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness?
And what, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is the loss of relatives?
Here, Master Raṭṭhapāla, a certain person has many friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relations."
Those relatives of his gradually come to an end.
He reflects thus:
"Formerly, I had many friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relations."
These [desires] of mine gradually came to an end.
Yet it was not easy for me to acquire wealth not yet acquired, nor to increase the wealth already acquired.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Thus, being possessed of that loss of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
This, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is called the loss of relatives.
Now, Master Raṭṭhapāla, you have many friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relations right here in Thullakoṭṭhita.
That loss of relatives does not apply to Master Raṭṭhapāla.
What has Master Raṭṭhapāla known, seen, or heard that he went forth from the home life into homelessness?
Indeed, Master Raṭṭhapāla, there are these four kinds of loss, possessed of which some here shave off their hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Those things do not exist for Master Raṭṭhapāla.
What has Master Raṭṭhapāla known, seen, or heard that he went forth from the home life into homelessness?

“There are, Great King, four summaries of the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—which I have known, seen, and heard, and because of which I went forth from the home life into homelessness.”
Which four?
“‘The world is swept away;

it is unstable,’ this, great king, was the first summary of the Dhamma proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, which I, having known, seen, and heard, went forth from the home life into homelessness.”

‘The world is without protection, without a refuge,’ this, great king, was the second summary of the Dhamma proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, which I, having known, seen, and heard, went forth from the home life into homelessness.
‘The world belongs to no one; everything must be abandoned and departed from.’

"Great King, this third summary of the Dhamma was proclaimed by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, after which I, having known it, seen it, and heard it, went forth from the home life into homelessness:
'The world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving.

Great King, this fourth summary of the Dhamma was proclaimed by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, after which I, having known it, seen it, and heard it, went forth from the home life into homelessness."

“Great King, these are the four summaries of the Dhamma taught by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—which I, having known, seen, and heard, went forth from the home life into homelessness.
“The world is swept away;
it is unstable,” said the venerable Raṭṭhapāla.
“Master Raṭṭhapāla, how is the meaning of this statement to be understood?
“What do you think, Great King?
When you were twenty years old or twenty-five years old, were you not skilled in elephant-riding and horse-riding?”
"Was he skilled in the chariot, skilled in the bow, skilled in the sword, possessed of strength in his thighs and strength in his arms, self-reliant, and capable in the theater of battle?
"I was, Master Raṭṭhapāla; when I was twenty years old and also when I was twenty-five years old, I was [skilled] even in the elephant."
“Skilled on horseback, skilled on chariot, skilled with the bow, skilled with the sword, strong of thigh,
strong of arm, self-reliant, and a veteran of battle—
sometimes, Master Raṭṭhapāla, I think I am even possessed of supernormal power; yet I do not see anyone who is my equal in strength.”
“What do you think, great king?
Are you now likewise strong of thigh, strong of arm, capable, and ready for the field of battle?
“Certainly not, Master Raṭṭhapāla.”
“Now I am old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the end of my life; my age has turned to eighty.
Sometimes, Master Raṭṭhapāla, when I think, ‘I will place my foot here,’ I place my foot elsewhere.
“This, great king, was said by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—with reference to this very thing.”
“The world is being led away;
it is unstable”—this is what I have known, seen, and heard, and having understood it, I went forth from the home life into homelessness.
“It is wonderful, Master Raṭṭhapāla! It is marvelous, Master Raṭṭhapāla!”
"How well this was said by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
'The world is swept away; it is unstable.
Indeed, Master Raṭṭhapāla, the world is swept away; it is unstable."
"Indeed, Master Raṭṭhapāla, in this royal family there exist elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry; they will serve to ward off our misfortunes.
Yet Master Raṭṭhapāla says: 'The world is without refuge, without a protector.'"
"But how, Master Raṭṭhapāla, should the meaning of this statement be understood?
"What do you think, Great King?
Do you have any chronic illness?"
“Master Raṭṭhapāla, I have a chronic illness.
Sometimes, Master Raṭṭhapāla, my friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations stand surrounding me, saying:
‘Now King Koravya will pass away; now King Koravya will pass away.’”
“What do you think, Great King?
Do you receive from your friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations [this request]:
‘Come, sirs, my friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations; may all of you together share this feeling of mine, so that I might experience only a lighter feeling’?”
“Or do you yourself experience that feeling?
“I cannot, Master Raṭṭhapāla, get my friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives to say:
‘Come, sirs, my friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives; all of you together share this feeling so that I may experience it as something much lighter.’”
“Then indeed, I alone experience that feeling.
“This, Great King, is what was spoken by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—with reference to this:
‘The world is without refuge, it has no protector.’”
"It is because I have known, seen, and heard this that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.
"It is wonderful, Master Raṭṭhapāla! It is marvelous, Master Raṭṭhapāla!
How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: [as you have said]."
‘The world is without protection, without refuge.
Indeed, Master Raṭṭhapāla, the world is without protection, without refuge.
Yet, Master Raṭṭhapāla, there exists in this royal family abundant gold and silver, both stored underground and kept above ground.
“The world is a burden; having abandoned everything, one must go”—thus has Master Raṭṭhapāla spoken.
But how, Master Raṭṭhapāla, is the meaning of this statement to be understood?”
“What do you think, Great King?
Just as you now enjoy yourself, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, will you obtain in the future:

‘In exactly this same way, I shall enjoy myself, endowed and possessed of these very same five strands of sensual pleasure,’ or rather, will others take possession of this wealth while you, however, go according to your own karma?”
“Master Raṭṭhapāla, although I am now provided with and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure and enjoy them, I shall not obtain even in the future:
‘May I be provided with and endowed with these very same five cords of sensual pleasure and enjoy them in this way.
Rather, others will take possession of this wealth, while I shall go according to my karma.”
“Indeed, Great King, it was with reference to this that the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One—spoke thus:
‘The world is without owner; having abandoned everything, one must go.
It is knowing this, seeing this, and hearing this, that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.”
“It is wonderful, Master Raṭṭhapāla! It is marvelous, Master Raṭṭhapāla!
How well this has been expressed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
‘The world is ownerless; having abandoned everything, one must go forth.’”
For it is true, Master Raṭṭhapāla, that this world must go on its way having abandoned everything.
"The world is deficient, unsatisfied, a slave to craving"—
this is what Master Raṭṭhapāla has said.
“Master Raṭṭhapāla, how is the meaning of this statement to be understood?
“What do you think, Great King?
Do you dwell in a prosperous Kuru country?”
“Yes, Master Raṭṭhapāla, I dwell in a prosperous kingdom.
“What do you think, Great King?
Suppose a man were to come here from the eastern direction, one who is trustworthy and reliable.”
Then, having approached him, he would say:
“Truly, great king, you should know this: I have come from the eastern direction.
There I saw a great country, prosperous and flourishing, populous and teeming with people.”
There were many there consisting of elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry;
there was much wealth and grain there;
and there was much gold and bullion, both unworked and worked.
“Therein there is much possession of women,
and it could be conquered with just that much strength.
Conquer it, Great King!”— what would you do in such a case?
“We too, Master Raṭṭhapāla, would conquer him and dwell there.
“What do you think, Great King?
Suppose a man were to come from the western direction…”
From the northern direction...
from the southern direction...
from across the great ocean, he is trustworthy and reliable.
Then, having approached him, he should say:
"Truly, Great King, you should know this: I have come from beyond the great ocean.
There I saw a vast country, prosperous and flourishing, with many people and teeming with inhabitants."
Therein were many bodies of elephants, bodies of horses, bodies of chariots, and bodies of infantry;
there was much wealth and grain;
and there was much gold and bullion, both worked and unworked.
“There are many women there as wives,
and it would be possible to conquer them with just that much strength.
Conquer them, Great King!”— what would you do in such a case?
“We too, Master Raṭṭhapāla, would conquer that [country] and dwell there.
“Great King, it was with reference to this that the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—said:
‘The world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving.’”
“Having known, seen, and heard this, I went forth from the home life into homelessness.
“It is wonderful, Master Raṭṭhapāla! It is marvelous, Master Raṭṭhapāla!
How well this has been spoken by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One:”
“The world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving.
“For indeed, Master Raṭṭhapāla, the world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving.
This is what the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said.
Having said this, he then spoke further:
“I see people in the world possessing wealth who,
having acquired riches, do not give them away out of delusion.”
Greedy, they accumulate wealth and desire even more sensual pleasures.
Even a king, having conquered the earth by force—
Dwelling upon the earth bounded by the oceans,
one who is not yet satisfied with what is on this side of the sea might still long for the further shore beyond the sea.
The king and many other people,
not free from craving, come to death;
being incomplete, they abandon the body.
There is no satiety with sensual pleasures in this world.
His kinsmen, tearing at their hair, wail for him, crying out, "Alas!
Oh, that he were not dead!"
Having carried him out wrapped in a cloth,
they take up the funeral pyre and burn him from there;
he is burned while being pierced by stakes.
When one has abandoned all wealth with but a single garment,
neither kinsmen, nor friends, nor companions here provide protection for one who is dying.
His heirs take away his wealth,
but the being goes wherever his karma leads;
when one dies, not a single thing follows after the wealth.
Sons, wives, wealth, and the kingdom—
through wealth one does not obtain long life,
nor can one ward off old age with riches.
The wise say that this life here is short,
impermanent, and subject to change.
Both the wealthy and the poor experience contact.
Both the fool and the wise man are touched by the same thing;
yet the fool lies prostrate, slain by his own foolishness,
while the wise man does not tremble when touched by contact.
Therefore, wisdom is indeed better than wealth,
by which one attains security in this world; for through a lack of such security,
one wanders from existence to existence.
Out of delusion they perform evil deeds;
entering the womb and the other world,
they undergo saṃsāra in continuous succession.
One who lacks wisdom, yet places full faith in this,
enters the womb and the next world,
like a thief caught at the mouth of a tunnel.
The one of evil nature is slain by his own deed;
even so, after passing away, in the world beyond,
the one of evil nature is slain by his own deed.
Sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful;
they agitate the mind with their diverse forms.
Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, [one should turn away].
Therefore, O King, I have gone forth.
Like the fruits of a tree, young men and old alike fall when their bodies break apart.
"Having seen this too, O King, I have gone forth;
the life of a recluse is undoubtedly better.
The Raṭṭhapāla Sutta is finished, the second.
